pr_title: Fix RequestBody logging when zero byte read is used

issue_context.title: Different logging behaviour between net 6 and 7 for Request Body in HttpLoggingMiddleware
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

If you allow the http-logger, which is running unter net 6 to log requests, it will log them as expected. But the same code unter net 7 shows just an empty value.

In .net 6
Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpLogging.HttpLoggingMiddleware: Information: RequestBody: Date=2023-03-15

In .net 7
Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpLogging.HttpLoggingMiddleware: Information: RequestBody:

My guess is that the https://github.com/dotnet/dotnet/blob/b5fc13cdacdec01bb18d3271d8606e96949943ad/src/runtime/src/libraries/System.IO.Pipelines/src/System/IO/Pipelines/StreamPipeReader.cs#L243 here is the issue.

If used with .net 6 the value of the property reader.UseZeroByteReads is false, but its true if using .net 7
this invokes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/bec278eabea54f63da15e10e654bdfa4168a2479/src/Middleware/HttpLogging/src/RequestBufferingStream.cs#L89 with an empty string and prevet logging the true value.

### Expected Behavior

In Log should be something like this
Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpLogging.HttpLoggingMiddleware: Information: RequestBody: Date=2023-03-15

### Steps To Reproduce

Here is the complete code: https://github.com/EnemyArea/BrokenAddHttpLoggingNet

**Program.cs**
```c#
builder.Services.AddHttpLogging(logging =>
{
    logging.LoggingFields = HttpLoggingFields.All;
    logging.MediaTypeOptions.AddText("application/x-www-form-urlencoded");
});

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseHttpLogging();
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();
```

**WeatherForecastController.cs**
```c#
[Route("bydate")]
[HttpPost]
public IEnumerable<WeatherForecast> GetWeatherForecastForDate([FromForm] WeatherForecastRequest request)
{
    return Enumerable.Range(1, 5).Select(index => new WeatherForecast
    {
        Date = request.Date.AddDays(index),
        TemperatureC = Random.Shared.Next(-20, 55),
        Summary = Summaries[Random.Shared.Next(Summaries.Length)]
    })
    .ToArray();
}

appsettings.Development.json
{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpLogging.HttpLoggingMiddleware": "Information"
    }
  }
}
```

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

7.0.101

review_comments: If we checked `res` instead we'd still need to check if `destination.IsEmpty`, because you could reach the end of the underlying stream which would give `res == 0`. So it's simpler just to check `destination.IsEmpty`.

I guess the one on line 60 should be updated for consistency. The reason I originally didn't change it is because zero-byte reads are almost always done via StreamPipeReader, which doesn't have a synchronous read so Read won't be called. And, by default ASP.NET Core doesn't allow synchronous reads on streams anyways.

But, if a user set the option to allow synchronous reads, and did `request.Body.Read(new byte[0])`, then they would hit this path. It would be really odd, since the whole point of zero-byte reads is to avoid allocating until the underlying stream has data, which would be an async operation if there was no data yet.

TLDR; I'll update it for consistency 😄
I was not reading this correctly.  "Zero-byte reads" refers to the case where the destination buffer is empty, rather than to the case where the stream writes zero bytes to the buffer.

Zero-byte reads allow code to wait for available data without providing a potentially big buffer while waiting.

For example:
1. Make zero byte read to wait for data to be available: `await stream.ReadAsync(Array.Empy<byte>())`
2. Zero-byte read returns when there is some data available.
3. Rent buffer from pool and read again with a buffer: `await stream.ReadAsync(oneMegabyteBuffer)`. It should return quickly, allowing the buffer to be returned to the pool quickly.

This prevents the problem of many large buffers waiting for data, causing pinning and fragmentation.

> TLDR; I'll update it for consistency 😄

Are zero-byte reads for sync `Stream.Read` a thing? I haven't use sync read methods in so long that I'm not sure.
I'm fine with asserting it never happens if that's the case.

> Are zero-byte reads for sync Stream.Read a thing?

I think they are, because lots of stream implementations just call the async api and block in Read, so they inherit the zero-byte read feature from the async code path.
Yes, be consistent for Read and ReadAsync.
